notes.b: The Republic's declaration of a republic in 1949 led Britain to confirm partition in law, and the issue of Northern Ireland shaped relations for the next 40 years.
points: The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 took effect on 18 April 1949, and Britain responded with the Ireland Act 1949.
The Ireland Act 1949 provided that Northern Ireland would remain part of the UK unless its parliament consented to a change, which made a united Ireland dependent on Northern Ireland's own vote.

The Irish government's anti-partition campaign, led by Taoiseach John A. Costello, asked for the return of the six counties, and it was supported by parliamentary resolutions and diplomatic efforts abroad.
Britain treated partition as a settled matter, and its government refused to discuss a united Ireland without the consent of the Northern parliament.
Most Irish exports, especially agricultural produce such as cattle, dairy products and eggs, went to the British market in the 1950s and 1960s.
British demand for Irish goods meant that economic policy in Dublin was closely tied to conditions in Britain.
Britain was also the main source of imports for Irish consumers, so currency and tariff decisions in London affected prices in the Republic.
The move to free trade in the 1960s, and the eventual entry of both states into the EEC, reduced this dependence over time (see the notes on the First Programme for Economic Expansion).

notes.b: The first meetings between an Irish Taoiseach and a Northern Ireland Prime Minister since partition took place in 1965.
points: Seán Lemass met Terence O'Neill in Belfast in January 1965, and O'Neill returned the visit in Dublin in February 1965.
The meetings were friendly and raised hopes of closer cooperation, but they did not produce a formal agreement on partition.
Unionists opposed the meetings, and some hardliners in Northern Ireland saw them as a threat to the Stormont government.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement, signed in December 1965, followed the same wave of cooperation.

notes.h: Lynch, the Troubles and the UK government
points: The Troubles escalated from 1969, and the Irish government's response was shaped by the Arms Crisis of 1970 (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).
Lynch condemned internment, introduced in August 1971, and Irish opposition to British security policy was expressed in statements at the United Nations and the EEC.
Bloody Sunday, on 30 January 1972, when British soldiers shot 14 civilians dead in Derry, caused outrage in the Republic.
The British embassy in Dublin was burned by a crowd on 2 February 1972, and the Irish government protested, but relations were not broken off.
The Heath government in London and the Lynch government in Dublin maintained contact through the crisis.

notes.h: Sunningdale and the Council of Ireland, 1973–1974
points: The Sunningdale Agreement was signed in December 1973 by the British and Irish governments and the main Northern Ireland parties.
It provided for a power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland and a Council of Ireland with powers over cooperation between north and south.
The Irish government accepted that Northern Ireland would remain part of the UK while a majority wished, but gained a formal role for the Republic in its affairs.
The Ulster Workers' Council strike of May 1974 brought down the power-sharing executive and ended the agreement.

notes.h: Joint EEC membership and the Thatcher years
points: Ireland and Britain both joined the EEC on 1 January 1973, a change that reduced trade barriers between them and tied both into a common market.
Margaret Thatcher became British Prime Minister in May 1979, and she and Charles Haughey held summit talks in Dublin in December 1980.

The 1980 summit issued a joint statement referring to the totality of relationships between the two islands, which was intended to cover Northern Ireland as well as the wider relations between Britain and Ireland.
The Falklands War of 1982 caused a rift, as the Irish government refused to join EEC sanctions against Argentina, and Thatcher was critical of the decision.

notes.b: The agreement signed by FitzGerald and Thatcher is the single most important development in Anglo-Irish relations in this period.
points: The Anglo-Irish Agreement was signed at Hillsborough, Co. Down, on 15 November 1985.

It gave the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs through an Anglo-Irish Intergovernmental Conference, while confirming that Northern Ireland would remain in the UK unless a majority wished otherwise.
The Ulster Unionists opposed the agreement, and their MPs resigned their seats in early 1986 in a protest that forced by-elections.
The agreement was supported by the SDLP and seen as a major step towards cooperation between the two governments.
By 1989 the Anglo-Irish Intergovernmental Conference was meeting regularly, with a secretariat based in Belfast (verify location).
Relations between the two governments were stable but not without disagreements over security and extradition.
Northern Ireland remained divided, and the Troubles continued with paramilitary violence on both sides.
Historians see the period as one in which the British and Irish governments moved from confrontation towards close, if sometimes difficult, cooperation.
Achievements: the Sunningdale Agreement and the Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Irish government a formal voice in Northern Ireland.
Limits: neither agreement ended partition or the violence in Northern Ireland, and unionist opposition blocked both in practice.
Contemporary view: nationalists welcomed the Irish government's role, while unionists saw it as a betrayal of the union.
Later view: historians see the Anglo-Irish Agreement as the foundation of the peace process, though its immediate success was limited.

The forum created by the 1985 agreement in which Irish and British ministers and officials discussed Northern Ireland.
